content: Home visits by healthcare staff or the use of digital technologies for daily communication can play a critical role in ensuring patients adhere to treatment, even when the treatment regimen is relatively short. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides recommendations on care and support for tuberculosis (TB) patients, which are available online in the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, specifically in Module 4: Treatment – Tuberculosis Care and Support. The BPALM/BPAL regimen includes bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, with or without moxifloxacin, administered throughout the treatment duration. Pretomanid is given at a dose of 200 mg once daily for the entire regimen. If moxifloxacin is included, it is dosed at 400 mg once daily. Moxifloxacin was the fluoroquinolone of choice in the TB-PRACTECAL trial, as no evidence supported the use of other fluoroquinolones at the time of the guideline development. Substituting moxifloxacin with levofloxacin or other fluoroquinolones is not recommended at this stage. Bedaquiline dosing schemes varied slightly between the TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials, but overall drug exposure was comparable. The TB-PRACTECAL trial followed the product label dosing schedule, while the ZeNix trial used a daily dosing schedule throughout the regimen, which may be an alternative option for administration. Two dosing schemes for bedaquiline are acceptable for programmatic implementation: (1) 200 mg once daily for 8 weeks, followed by 100 mg once daily; or (2) 400 mg once daily for 2 weeks as a loading dose, followed by 200 mg three times per week. Linezolid dosing in the ZeNix trial aimed to identify the optimal administration schedule due to its potential for serious adverse effects, including peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, and myelosuppression. The optimal dosing identified was 600 mg once daily for 26 weeks, with a reduction to 300 mg daily allowed in cases of linezolid-specific toxicities. In the TB-PRACTECAL trial, participants received 600 mg daily for 16 weeks, followed by 300 mg daily for the remaining 8 weeks (total duration: 24 weeks). The panel recommended using 600 mg daily throughout the regimen, with the option to reduce to 300 mg daily if toxicity occurs. The BPALM and BPAL regimens have been studied as standardized treatment courses. Modifications, such as early discontinuation or replacement of any component medicines, may lead to suboptimal treatment outcomes. In the TB-PRACTECAL trial, patients received 24 weeks of BPALM. In the ZeNix trial, treatment was extended to 9 months for patients who remained sputum culture-positive or reverted to being culture-positive between months 4 and 6, or whose clinical condition suggested progressive TB. Eligible patients with fluoroquinolone susceptibility can start the BPALM regimen for 6 months, with dosing as described above. If resistance to fluoroquinolones is identified, moxifloxacin can be discontinued. The BPAL regimen can be extended to 39 weeks in cases of failure to convert culture between months 4 and 6 or based on clinical judgment. Up to 1 month can be added to the overall treatment duration to compensate for missed doses. Missed doses and treatment interruptions should be minimized. If interruptions occur, consecutive interruptions of up to 2 weeks or non-consecutive missed doses totaling up to 4 weeks should be made up by extending the treatment duration. After 9 weeks of consecutive linezolid administration at 600 mg daily, the dose can be reduced to 300 mg daily or omitted for up to 8 weeks if intolerability occurs, while continuing other medicines in the regimen. If any of these tolerances are exceeded, a thorough assessment of the patient’s status is required to decide whether to continue or modify the treatment strategy. Patients on BPALM/BPAL regimens require baseline testing and regular clinical and laboratory monitoring during treatment. Monthly sputum cultures are recommended for patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). Failure to convert sputum culture by the fourth month of treatment may indicate a failing regimen. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) for fluoroquinolones is essential to guide the prescription of BPALM or BPAL regimens and prevent unnecessary toxicity. Countries are encouraged to establish DST capacity for bedaquiline and linezolid resistance testing, particularly in cases of fluoroquinolone resistance or lack of bacteriological conversion after month 4. Clinicians should monitor for adverse events such as hepatotoxicity (e.g., fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, hepatomegaly), peripheral or optic neuropathy, and conduct laboratory tests (e.g., ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, complete blood count, serum potassium, calcium, magnesium). An ECG should be obtained before treatment initiation. A suggested monitoring schedule is provided in the operational handbook on drug-resistant TB treatment. The WHO framework for active TB drug-safety monitoring and management (aDSM) should be applied to all MDR-TB regimens to ensure adequate monitoring for adverse events and prompt responses, alongside monitoring for treatment outcomes and early signs of treatment failure. Additional evidence on adverse events will be critical to building the safety profile of new regimens in diverse settings. Monitoring changes in linezolid dosing and duration will also inform the evidence base for the broader use of BPALM/BPAL regimens and linezolid tolerability. Research priorities include evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of BPALM/BPAL regimens in subpopulations with limited data (e.g., children under 14, patients with extrapulmonary TB, people living with HIV with CD4 counts below 100, pregnant and lactating women), gathering data from additional regions, understanding pretomanid resistance mechanisms, documenting adverse event profiles, exploring the relative efficacy of pretomanid and delamanid, and investigating geographical differences in linezolid-related adverse events. Further research is also needed to explore replacing moxifloxacin with levofloxacin, cross-resistance between bedaquiline and clofazimine, resistance monitoring for new medicines, methods to ensure treatment adherence, and the efficacy of other 6-month regimens.
